ut_la_sal_mountains.blurb: The La Sal Mountains rise above Moab in southeast Utah, and the crags sit high up, which makes them a cooler alternative to the desert climbing below. Sport routes lead the way, followed by trad and a sizeable group of boulder problems, with a handful of top-rope and ice lines. Most roped climbs fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with fewer easier routes, and boulder problems run from V0 to about V8. Mill Creek is the biggest sub-area, built on compact sandstone and quartzite that favors face climbing; the ratings there are stiff and holds are often sandy. The Dakota crags, Hideout Wall and North Fork add more variety. Climbing is mainly a summer proposition.

va_great_falls.blurb: Great Falls lines the Potomac River's Mather Gorge, roughly fifteen miles northwest of Washington, DC, with most of the cliffs on the Virginia side and a smaller number across the river in Maryland. The rock is mica schist, and it can feel slick. Cliffs are short, around 20 to 60 feet, and the climbing is mostly face climbing with sparse natural protection, so top-roping is the usual approach, alongside a good amount of traditional climbing and a few boulders and scrambles. Grades run from 5.0 through the low 5.12s, but the bulk sit between 5.6 and 5.10. Dihedrals, Aid Box and Cow's Hoof are among the larger crags. High river water cuts off some walls.

va_hkl_west.blurb: HKL West is the western side of High Knob Landform, a large, wet massif in the Cumberland Mountains of Southwest Virginia that tops 4,000 feet. It is all bouldering, on very hard sandstone blocks scattered through the forest. Most problems fall between V0 and V6, with the heart of the range around V2 to V5 and a thinner tail up to V11. Keokee Lake holds the large majority of the problems, Cliff Mountain Boulders adds a set of low and medium blocks with a few highballs, and Devil's Boulders is small. With heavy rain and snowfall through the year, conditions vary a lot, and the setting is quiet and remote.

bc_chek.blurb: Chek is the main sport-climbing zone of Cheakamus Canyon, in the Sea to Sky corridor of British Columbia, roughly 25 km north of Squamish beside the highway. Nearly everything is bolted, and the grades lean hard: the bulk sit between 5.10 and 5.12, with a good number of 5.13s, a few 5.14s, and a modest set of 5.8 and 5.9 climbs for those warming up. The crag is split into many sectors; Electric Avenue is the biggest, followed by Forgotten Wall, The Monastery and The Circus. It sits close to the road yet is shielded from road noise, so it feels more tucked away than it is.

co_glenwood_canyon.blurb: Glenwood Canyon is the Colorado River gorge along I-70 east of Glenwood Springs, where layers of limestone and old granite are exposed. Sport climbing dominates, with a solid base of trad and some bouldering. Most roped climbs fall between 5.9 and 5.12, with fewer easy ones and a few 5.13s, and boulder problems run from V0 to V5. Puoux is the main limestone sport crag, split into several sections and climbable year round. No Name Canyon is a side canyon of single-pitch granite cracks. Ice and mixed routes form in cold winters, and high water can complicate reaching the granite walls.

ma_middlesex_fells.blurb: Middlesex Fells is a wooded reservation just north of Boston, packed with boulders and short walls. Bouldering makes up most of it, with a smaller set of top-rope and trad climbs and the occasional ice line. Problems are mostly easy to moderate, V0 to V4, with a thin tail reaching V9, while top-rope and trad climbing runs about 5.2 to 5.10. Red Cross Path Vicinity, Wright's Park and Hemlock Pool hold the best-known boulders, many a few minutes' walk from the trails, while Black and White Rocks has small crags up to about 80 feet that suit beginners. Local climbers favor natural lines over contrived ones.
